13: Big D for big arms! Created for expert players and windy conditions, NUKE OS (Over Stable) is a super fast driver that rewards power throwers with insane distance potential. 27: From Dynamic Discs: A versatile high-speed disc is hard to find. They are usually too far on one side of the spectrum to be a true multi-tool. Introducing the Sheriff by Dynamic Discs. 28: The problem with the highest speed discs is that they are historically understable. This is no longer an issue. The Defender is here. Fast. Stable. 29: The Enforcer is Dynamic Discs flagship overstable distance driver. Similar in flight to Discmania's PD2, the Enforcer is slightly less overstable than the Dynamic Discs General.
30: The Dynamic Discs Trespass is a high-speed distance driver designed to offer a neutral flight path, making it suitable for players seeking both distance and control. 31: The Renegade is a controllable understable distance driver from Dynamic Discs, great for long turnovers, tailwind shots, and max-distance lines for slower arms. With a touch of high-speed turn and reliable fade, it offers easy distance without sacrificing control. First released in 2013, it remains a reliable option for players who want glide and workability in one package.
32: The Dynamic Discs Criminal is an overstable fairway driver, introduced in 2017, designed for players seeking a reliable disc in challenging conditions. With more glide than the Felon and greater stability than the Convict, the Criminal offers a dependable flight path for both backhand and forehand throws. Its consistent fade and resistance to turn make it suitable for headwinds and power throws. Although the Criminal has been retired from production, it remains a valued disc among players who appreciate its unique flight characteristics.
35: The Dynamic Discs Escape debuted in 2012 as a Speed 9 fairway driver that brought smooth glide and effortless release to all skill levels. It offers a touch of turn before finishing straight, making it ideal for hyzer-flips, flex lines, and even rollers. Compared to its more overstable sibling, the Getaway, the Escape is more playable for developing arms and excels when you want flight but not too much fade. Players often describe it as “glidey and forgiving,” with newer throwers praising its ease, and experienced players valuing it as a consistent 300‑foot control tool. If you're looking for a friendly yet capable fairway driver, the Escape fits the bill.
36: A slightly understable fairway driver that blends the comfortable feel of a midrange with the reach of a fairway. It offers a smooth ride with mild turn before settling into a gentle fade—perfect for when you need a bit more distance but still demand accuracy. Its reliable holding of anhyzer lines and ability to fly straight make it a solid go-to for both beginners and experienced players seeking controlled flight and versatility.
37: The Dynamic Discs Thief is a dependable control/fairway driver suited for a wide range of players. It delivers a stable-to-straight flight with enough glide to cover fairway gaps cleanly. For those with slower arm speed, it leans overstable—offering predictable fade—while stronger arms can coax a straight shot with a mild hyzer release. It’s the kind of mold you toss when you want a trustworthy line-driver that adapts to how you throw it.
38: Dynamic Discs’ Witness was the Trilogy era’s beginner-friendly fairway: PDGA-approved on February 17, 2014, and beloved for effortless hyzer-flips, gentle turnovers, and tailwind control. It has a comfy, narrowish rim and tons of glide, but it rewards finesse—power it flat and it can “turn and burn,” while a touch of hyzer sends it laser-straight before a soft finish. Lightweight runs (like Lucid Air) were especially flippy and popular for stand-ups and easy rollers. Though the Witness has since been retired from regular production, fans still chase its flight in close cousins like the Underworld or Essence. 47: The Captain is definitly up there on the list of farthest flying discs in Disc Golf Valley. In real life it's not much different, it goes very far, and is great for S-Curve distance shots.
50: The Dynamic Discs Getaway launched in late 2017 as a step up in stability from the popular Escape—ideal for players craving that Escape feel but needing a disc that won’t turn over. It flies straight and holds a subtle fade, making it a dependable mid-range bomber or controlled fairway tool. Compared to the Escape, it resists torque and handles wind with more authority, yet maintains similar glide. Reviewers often say it’s become their “go-to” fairway when they want a touch more security without sacrificing that familiar feel. If you’ve ever loved your Escape but outgrew its stability, the Getaway is your upgrade.
56: The Ape can handle the raw, primal power of disc golfs biggest arms. Extremely fast and stable, the Ape is a "must have" distance driver for windy conditions and sharp doglegs. Sidearm drivers will learn the Ape is more than capable of standing up to even the most intense torque. The Ape is an outstanding choice for backhand or sidearm throws as well as a variety of niche flex shots. With less high speed turn than a Boss, the Ape is not recommended for players who throw less than 300ft.
57: Nate Sexton's forehand distance driver of choice. The XCal has a slightly more comfortable feel in the hand for forehand shots than the Destroyer, and its added overstability helps make it more torque resistant.
58: The Boss is the disc that distance throwers take out into the desert to smash as far as they can. In a ripping 50-60mph tailwind, distances upwards of 1000+ feet are possible, from people with elite armspeed of course. Slightly faster than the Destroyer, the Boss has some insane distance potential. All that, combined with consistant overstability you can totally count on.
59: I would love to see what David Wiggins Jr. could do with one of these. I bet he could smash a Colossus farther than a Boss. The Colossus is fast, and with that kind of speed comes a dash of inconsistancy. Sure, this disc may land farther down-field than your Destroyer, but can you control it?

61: The most popular and most emulated distance driver of all time. The flight numbers 12/5/-1/3 are the staple for a good distance driver, and credit is due to the Destroyer for that. If you can handle it, the Destroyer has the potential to fly far and consistant. But are you ready?
62: The Shryke bombs, no doubt about it. A slightly faster disc than the classic Innova Tern, the Shryke delivers easy turn, lots of glide, and a consistant finish. It's also a main production distance driver, meaning it's available in tons of different plastics.
63: The Dominator was axed from Innovas main lineup because of overcrowding in their 13-speed category. It was never an imensely popular disc, and has since been replaced in the lineup by the Charger. You may still be able to get your hands on a Dominator from the Innova Factory Store, which sometimes has out of production discs avialable.
64: The TeeDevil is a high-speed distance driver designed to offer big distance with control. It features a wide rim and low profile, providing a comfortable grip for powerful throws. With less fade than the Destroyer, the TeeDevil allows for precise control over distance drives, making it an ideal choice for players seeking a reliable go-to driver. While the TeeDevil is not currently in regular production, it remains a sought-after disc for those who appreciate its unique flight characteristics. Players looking for a disc with similar performance might consider the Wraith, which offers a comparable blend of speed and control.
65: The Innova Tern is a high-speed, understable distance driver designed for players seeking maximum distance with less effort. Its combination of speed and glide makes it suitable for intermediate players aiming to achieve long, controlled flights. The Terns understable nature allows for smooth turnovers and hyzer-flip shots, making it a versatile choice for various shot shapes. Compared to other Innova drivers, the Tern offers more turn and glide, positioning it between the Archon and the Katana in terms of stability. Its particularly effective for tailwind shots and long anhyzers, providing a reliable option for players looking to add distance without requiring maximum power. The Tern is available in multiple plastic blends, including Star, GStar, and Champion, each offering different grip and durability characteristics. Notably, the Champion plastic version is slightly more stable, providing a touch more control for players with higher arm speeds. 66: The Innova Wahoo is a high-speed distance driver designed for long-range throws over water, featuring a unique ability to float. With a wide 2.4 cm rim and substantial glide, it offers a flight path similar to the Dragon but with increased speed and range. The Wahoos understable nature allows for smooth turnovers and hyzer-flip shots, making it a versatile choice for various shot shapes. Available in R-Pro plastic, the Wahoo provides excellent grip in all weather conditions. Its floating capability makes it an ideal choice for courses with significant water hazards, offering players confidence when throwing over larger bodies of water. While the Wahoo shares flight characteristics with discs like the Tern, it stands out with its floating feature, catering to players seeking both distance and water safety.
67: My father and I have a nickname for the Katana - The Heartbreaker. The reason we call it that is because it can be a little unpredictable for higher arm speeds. Lower armspeed throwers and older/younger/newer players will love the Katana for its effortless distance and glide. It has the potential to be the farthest flying disc in your bag.
68: The Daedalus is a slightly more understable disc than the Katana. Super understable discs like this are great more in tailwinds, as they'll flip a little less and carry forward a long way. In a headwind, discs like this tend to buckle.
69: Innova's most understable 13-speed disc. If you're having trouble getting turn out of this one, then you're probably not ready for 13-speed discs yet. The Vulcan is also made in a full range of weights in most plastics.
70: The Innova Wraith is a stable, high-speed distance driver that offers a balance of speed, glide, and control. With a speed rating of 11, it provides significant distance potential while maintaining a manageable rim width, making it accessible for a wide range of players. The Wraith's flight characteristics include a slight turn and a reliable fade, allowing for versatile shot shaping, including hyzer flips and long anhyzers. Compared to the Innova Destroyer, the Wraith requires less power to achieve full flight, making it a suitable choice for intermediate players seeking to extend their distance capabilities. Its performance in various wind conditions and adaptability to both forehand and backhand throws have solidified its place as a staple in many disc golfers' bags.
71: The Krait is a stable, high-speed distance driver from Innova, offering a straight flight with a gentle fade. With flight numbers of 11/5/-1/2, it provides a balance of speed and control, making it suitable for players seeking consistent distance. The Krait's design allows for effective performance in various conditions, including headwinds and forehand throws. Its unique rim shape contributes to its reliable flight path, making it a versatile choice for many players.
72: The Archon blends the long-turning flight of a Katana with the gentle finish of a Wraith. It’s a speed 11 driver that offers glide and workability, great for shaping S-curves and hyzer flips. Best suited for intermediate arms seeking max distance with a touch of finesse.
73: The Innova Mystere is a smooth-flying distance driver that excels at carving long, controlled S-curves. It offers a gentle high-speed turn and reliable fade, making it ideal for players seeking effortless distance and precise shot shaping. Whether you're navigating tight fairways or open courses, the Mystere provides consistent performance and adaptability.
74: The Innova Mamba is a high-speed distance driver introduced in 2012, designed to provide maximum distance with minimal effort. Its significant high-speed turn and exceptional glide make it ideal for players with lower arm speeds seeking to achieve longer flights. The Mamba excels in tailwind conditions, hyzer flips, and long turnover shots, offering a reliable option for shaping precise lines. Notably, five-time World Champion Juliana Korver has utilized the Mamba in her game, highlighting its effectiveness for controlled distance throws.
75: The Innova Orc is a speed 10 distance driver introduced in 2004, designed to offer a balanced blend of speed, glide, and control. With its moderate fade and slight turn, it excels in long, straight shots and controlled hyzer lines, making it suitable for both backhand and forehand throws. The Orc's design allows it to perform reliably in various wind conditions, providing a dependable option for players seeking consistency in their distance drives. Notably, the Orc was among the first discs to feature Innova's Champion plastic, enhancing its durability and performance. While it may not be as prominent in modern lineups, the Orc remains a favorite among players who appreciate its versatility and reliable flight characteristics.
76: The Innova Starfire is a dependable distance driver introduced in 2003, designed for players seeking a balance of speed and control. With its consistent fade and moderate glide, it excels in headwind conditions, hyzer lines, and controlled S-curves. The Starfire's design allows for precise shot shaping, making it a reliable choice for both backhand and forehand throws. Notably, 12-time world champion Ken Climo has utilized the Starfire in his competitive play, highlighting its effectiveness at the highest levels of the sport.
77: Bringing back the original, more stable mold! Originally Posted by Innova Customer Service: “Thank you for throwing INNOVA. It appears the main question here is: Will Beasts only be produced with the new “old mold”? The answer is yes. Here is the whole story which should answer all of your other concerns. The Beast was created in late 2002. After Barry Schultz won his second world championship in 2004, Dave Dunipace made a slight change to the Beast mold to make it a little less high speed stable than the original. He felt the original Beast was too similar to the Orc. Since the original mold was retooled, we have only able to produce the new retooled Beast. In 2014, problems arose with the Beast. Malfunctioning mold parts could no longer be used and were retired. We ordered new Beast parts from our mold making company. They mistakenly produced the Beast from the original disc specifications and not from the updated 2004 specifications. So now we have a new “old mold” Beast. Barry Schultz was very happy about it as he got his beloved original Beast back. Since we can no longer make the Beast with the faulty retooled parts, every Beast going forward will be made with the new “old mold”. It is possible some retailers will continue to have older Beasts in stock until they sell out. The flight numbers on the Beast will remain unchanged as they accurately reflect the flight of the current version of the Beast. Collectors will be able tell an original old mold from the new old mold as the new mold does not have patent numbers. The only way to tell the difference between the retooled mold and the new “old mold” Beasts is by the shape of the rim. Most Beast throwers and savvy collectors are already aware of these facts. Again, all Beasts going forward will be made in the new “old mold”. “
78: The Innova Monarch is a glide-hungry understable distance driver that’s earned a spot in many bags as a dependable roller and turnover bomber. It has a smooth, rounded rim that lends itself well to both backhand and forehand throws—especially those silky rollers that just won’t quit. One Redditor praised it for delivering “beautifully understable and exceptionally glidey” flights, while others report consistent performance even on power tosses. Ideal for players stepping up into faster discs, the Monarch gives beginners extra distance and advanced players a reliable roller companion. Think of it as your launchpad to long, flowing tunnels or breeze-assisted tailwind shots.
79: The Innova Firebird is more than just a disc—it’s a legend. Released in 2000, it quickly became the blueprint for overstable fairway drivers. Trusted by pros and ams alike, it’s known for its fierce fade, wind-fighting reliability, and a forehand feel that’s second to none. Whether you're spiking it into the green or flexing through a headwind, the Firebird delivers with brutal consistency. It’s been a staple in countless pro bags for decades—and with good reason. If you need control, fade, and a disc that’s earned its stripes over 20+ years, the Firebird is always up to the task.
80: The Innova Thunderbird debuted in 2014 as a Speed 9 fairway driver designed to merge control and power. It combines the dependable stability of a TeeBird with the glide of a Valkyrie, offering a balanced flight that stays true under pressure—especially in wind. It’s often described as a “seasoned Firebird with less fade,” making it a go-to for placement shots requiring both distance and precision. Power throwers enjoy its ability to flex through gaps before settling into a smooth finish, while average arms benefit from its predictability. If you're searching for a versatile utility driver that handles crosswinds and slight turn flawlessly, the Thunderbird delivers. The Thunderbird was the disc Paul McBeth used for his famouns ESPN aired ace:
81: The Innova Viking is a workhorse control driver that delivers clean, straight lines with a dependable fade. It’s often overlooked in favor of flashier molds, but those who bag it know how reliable it is for both backhand and forehand throws. The Viking holds its angle with confidence, resisting unwanted turn without feeling overly dumpy at the finish. Players with smooth form or moderate power find it especially useful for tight fairways, tunnel shots, and precision placement drives. Its flight is predictable and versatile—enough stability to trust in wind, but not so much that it sacrifices glide. The Viking has quietly built a loyal following as a no-nonsense option for consistent control without drama.
82: The Innova Valkyrie is a legendary control driver known for its effortless glide and easy distance. Once the world record holder for longest throw, it continues to be a go-to for players who want a disc that naturally shapes S-curves and tailwind bombs without excessive effort. Its turn makes it perfect for hyzer flips, gentle turnovers, and rollers, especially as it beats in. Beginners love it for its manageable feel and forgiving flight, while experienced throwers appreciate its workability and range of shot shapes. Though plastic types and runs can slightly affect stability, the Valkyrie consistently delivers on smooth, controlled distance with a reliable fade. It’s a classic for a reason—versatile, comfortable in the hand, and a staple in countless bags.
83: The Innova Sidewinder has been a mainstay in Innova’s lineup since the early 2000s, admired for its glide-rich understable flight and ability to shape effortless long turnovers and rollers. It reliably delivers a predictable high-speed turn when thrown flat or on hyzer, then gently fades—offering a flight path that's both exciting and forgiving. Many players report it feels like a first driver for those building power, yet still proves useful for finesse shots and controlled placement. Premium plastics, such as Champion or Halo Star, add longevity and slightly more resistance to turning, but they still beat in to reveal that signature smooth, glide-first performance. Lightweight DX or GStar runs are especially popular among newer players for their ease and ready-for-rollers turn. After two decades, the Sidewinder remains a go-to understable shape driver that's easy to throw and fun to shape—ideal for rollers, turnovers, and carefree distance.
84: The Innova Roadrunner is a long-standing favorite for players who value glide, finesse, and control. Since its release in 2005, it has earned a reputation for delivering smooth hyzer-flips, effortless turnovers, and dependable rollers. The Roadrunner excels when thrown with a touch of hyzer, flipping up to flat before gliding down the fairway with a gentle finish. It’s a top choice for players with slower arm speeds looking to add distance, but experienced throwers also rely on it for carving precise lines through tight fairways or launching tailwind bombs. Compared to similar discs, it offers more high-speed turn and less fade, making it especially useful for shaping wide S-curves and laying down consistent rollers. Its versatility, reliability, and approachable flight make it a long-time staple in bags across all skill levels.
85: The Innova Teebird3 is a refined evolution of the classic Teebird—a point-and-shoot fairway driver with a sleeker, flatter profile that cuts through wind better and flies a touch faster. It retains the dependable, dead-straight flight and dependable fade the Teebird is famous for, but the flatter top gives it extra torque resistance and precision. Many players choose it for long, anhyzer-release S-curves or tight tunnel shots where wind and control are factors. Compared to the original Teebird, the Teebird3 feels slightly faster and more stable, yet still remains smooth and reliable. It's a go-to for those who want accuracy and consistency with just a whisper more bite in challenging conditions—perfect when fade and finesse matter most.
87: Innova’s Dragon is the classic “safety-net” driver for water holes—a lightweight-only, floating fairway made from a buoyant, super-grippy blend that stays on top if it splashes down. The comfortable, modest rim suits newer arms, and the flight rewards touch: a little hyzer pops to flat and glides straight, while gentle turnovers come easy for shaping lines through the woods or riding tailwinds. Veterans keep one for worry-free carries when the penalty for a miss is a swim. The tradeoff is durability and wind resistance; it beats in quickly and doesn’t love headwinds or big power. Among Innova’s floaters, the Dragon remains the friendliest everyday thrower—fun, forgiving, and famously unsinkable.
88: Innova’s Archangel is a classic beginner-friendly control driver from 2001, built to make hyzer-flips, long drifting turnovers, and easy distance feel automatic. A comfortable, modest rim and mostly-lightweight DX runs keep it approachable out of the hand; out of the box it stands up from a touch of hyzer, rides straight, and settles gently. Power throwers often beat one in as a woods roller or late-turn specialist, while newer players appreciate how forgiving it is at lower speeds. The trade-offs are typical: DX seasons quickly and it doesn’t love headwinds or heavy torque. Premium runs have appeared here and there, but the Archangel’s reputation was made in DX.
89: Innova’s Banshee is an old-school overstable fairway from the late 1990s that earned a reputation as a forehand-friendly, wind-beating workhorse before “meathook” became a marketing term. With a comfortable, modest rim and minimal glide, it excels at forced hyzers, skip shots, and point-and-dump placements that need to finish now, not later. Power it flat and it shrugs off torque; power it down and it lands on a dime—great in the woods where ground play matters. DX versions season into straighter line-holders (even rollers for big arms), while beefier premium and fundraiser runs stayed famously stout. Quietly, it’s still the utility fairway many players never took out of the bag.
90: Innova’s Teebird is the template for modern fairways: a straight, point-and-shoot driver with dependable late bite that earned its reputation in the late ’90s and never left the top tier. A comfortable, compact rim makes it equally at home on low ceilings, tight tunnels, and mild headwinds, while the finish is honest—confident without being dumpy—so placements stick where you call them. Run lore matters: early CE and 11x-era Teebirds are legendary for their crisp stability, DX beats into laser lines, and Champion/Star tend to start stout and season into trusty workhorses. The TL/TL3 spin-offs take the fade down a notch, and the Teebird3 trims dome for a faster, flatter feel. When you need fairway truth, the Teebird tells it.
142: The Nuke SS is essentially Discraft's answer to the Innova Katana. SS versions of Discraft discs are more understable. For example, the Nuke SS is more understable than the regular Nuke.
143: The Crank has a fairly narrow rim for a 13-speed. Don't be fooled, it's still a wide rim driver, but relative to the other 13-speeds it's a little less bulky in the hand. The Crank goes stupid far.
144: The SS version of the Crank, meaning it's more understable than the regular Crank. Higher armspeeds probably won't see much of a fade out of this disc. Lower armspeeds may thrive with the Crank SS. Its understability makes it exceptionally easy to throw.
147: The Thrasher is a fast, understable distance driver that offers impressive distance potential for players with moderate arm speed. It provides a smooth, controllable turn without being overly flippy, making it suitable for hyzer flips, long anhyzers, and tailwind drives. Compared to Discraft's Hades, the Thrasher offers a similar flight but with a slightly more neutral finish, making it a versatile choice for various skill levels.
149: The Discraft Avenger, introduced in 2005, was an overstable distance driver that gained prominence when Nate Doss used it to secure his 2005 World Championship title. Known for its reliable stability and consistent fade, the Avenger was a go-to choice for players seeking control in various wind conditions. Though discontinued in the late 2010s, the Avenger remains a sought-after disc among enthusiasts and collectors. Its legacy continues through the Avenger SS, a more understable variant that caters to a broader range of players. Additionally, the Discraft Anax offers a similar flight profile, providing players with modern alternatives that capture the essence of the original Avenger.
150: The Surge is a stable-to-overstable distance driver from Discraft, offering a balance of speed, glide, and control. With flight numbers of 11/5/-1/3, it provides a reliable fade and moderate turn, making it suitable for both backhand and forehand throws. The Surge's design allows for effective performance in various conditions, including headwinds. Often compared to the Innova Wraith, the Surge offers similar flight characteristics with a touch more overstability.
151: The Discraft Surge SS is a distance driver designed for players seeking maximum distance with less effort. With flight numbers of 11/5/-1/2, it offers a slight high-speed turn followed by a reliable fade, making it suitable for shaping S-curves and achieving long, controlled flights. The Surge SS is known for its impressive glide and smooth, easy-to-control turn, providing versatility for both backhand and forehand throws. Its a preferred choice for players looking to achieve long distances without requiring elite power.
153: Overstable! That’s the main word when describing the Stiletto. And that is OVERSTABLE with a capital everything. The Stiletto was designed based on feedback from pro disc golfers who wanted a disc so overstable that it could hold up to anything. When you are standing on the tee and the wind roars in your face, you will be relieved to find this disc in your bag. It cuts the air like a knife, flies fast and you know which way it is heading. When the storms are gathering – trust the Stiletto.
156: The Machete is Discraft’s go-to for extreme overstability—perfect for spike hyzers, skip shots, and battling headwinds. Its flat top and low profile make it a reliable choice for both forehand and backhand throws, delivering a consistent, hard fade every time. If you need a disc that cuts through the wind like its namesake, the Machete won't let you down.
157: Tired of choosing between speed and accuracy on the disc golf course? With the Ballista from Latitude 64 you can get the best of two worlds. One of the fastest discs in the world combined with a dependable flight path makes the Ballista a must-have in your bag. It will be overstable for beginners and slightly understable for experienced players.
158: The Discraft Avenger SS is the people’s turnover driver—easy to throw, hard not to love. 160: The Discraft Vulture is a speed 10 overstable control driver introduced in 2018. Designed as a seasoned Predator with added glide, it offers a reliable flight path with a consistent fade, making it suitable for both backhand and forehand throws. The Vulture's design allows for controlled distance shots, excelling in headwind conditions and providing confidence in various shot shapes. With its moderate rim width and comfortable feel, the Vulture is accessible to a wide range of players. It serves as a versatile option for those seeking a dependable driver that bridges the gap between fairway and distance drivers. Notably, the Vulture has been featured in Discraft's Tour Series, including the 2025 Holyn Handley Z Swirl edition, highlighting its continued relevance and popularity among professional players.
161: The Halo is a high speed, long range distance driver.
164: The Havoc has some crazy distance potential. We think it's more understable than the flight numbers suggest, but being a 13 sped it still takes a fast arm to truly activate it.
165: The Discraft Predator arrived in the early 2000s as Discraft’s first true answer to high-overstable fairway needs—and it remains a go-to. If you're after a disc with both legacy and backbone, the Predator delivers.
166: When speed is of the essence the Knight will ride with haste. This high-speed driver features one of the widest rims on a golf disc. 168: The Bolt is one of Latitude 64's most understable distance drivers. While it is certainly flippy, it still has a fade of 3, meaning it should consistantly come back and fade regardless of release angle. Slower arm speeds will have a field day throwing this disc, it'll go far for you.
169: The Flow is a high-speed distance driver known for its exceptional glide and smooth, controllable flight. With a domey top and wide rim, it offers a comfortable grip and impressive lift, making it ideal for long, straight drives. Often compared to a faster fairway driver, the Flow provides a dependable flight path with minimal fade, excelling in tailwind conditions and for players seeking maximum distance with less effort.

Offering a little turn before a controlled fade, it excels at hyzer-flips that straighten out, dependable headwind drives, and tunnel hyzers. Early runs felt like a speedy Stalker, later ones grew more stable—perfect for both developing and advanced arms. Seasoned players compare its glide-fade combo to a seasoned Teebird or Thunderbird with more versatility. If you want a fairway driver that delivers effortless distance with trusted finishes, the Undertaker deserves a spot in your bag.
171: The Discraft Mantis is a fairway driver that blends a compact rim with surprisingly smooth glide and a controlled, understable flight. It’s versatile enough for newer players using it as a distance driver, while more experienced players appreciate it for shot shaping—be it hyzer-flips, gentle turnovers, or holding a straight line on slower throws. With a comfortable feel and a flight profile that responds predictably to your pace, the Mantis earns its place as a go-to utility driver that sidesteps drama and delivers consistent performance.
172: Discraft’s Xpress debuted in December 2000 as one of the company’s early understable control drivers, prized for easy hyzer-flips, long drifting anhyzers, and effortless rollers. It has a smaller, comfortable rim that suits developing arms and woods golf, standing up from a touch of hyzer and gliding for days before settling gently. Power throwers treat it as a touch driver or roller machine, while newer players appreciate how forgiving it feels at lower speeds. Though the Xpress left regular production years ago, it pops back up in occasional limited runs—most notably a 2021 Ledgestone ESP release—so fans still chase that classic “slow Heat” flight. Old-school Z runs are quietly collectible, too.
173: The Thought Space Athletics Coalesce debuted in 2022 as a reliably stable fairway driver built for versatility and control. It offers a balanced flight—neutral enough for straight shots with power, but dependable when you need a late fade. Compared to TSA’s Omen, the Coalesce is less beefy and more workable, giving players a trustworthy option for shaping lines in both calm and breezy conditions. The flat top and smooth rim suit a variety of grips, making it a comfortable choice for both forehand and backhand throws. If you’re looking for a smart, balanced fairway driver, the Coalesce lives up to its name.
175: The Latitude 64 Saint Pro is a stable, control-focused fairway driver that offers a straighter, more torque-resistant alternative to the original Saint. While the Saint leans understable and excels at glidey turnover shots, the Saint Pro brings added stability and a firmer finish, making it better suited for powerful throws and headwind conditions. It handles both backhand and forehand lines well, with a smooth release and consistent fade. Players appreciate its ability to hold long, straight flights without drifting off-line, especially in wooded courses or tight landing zones. The Saint Pro is ideal for those who loved the feel of the Saint but wanted something that could handle more power without flipping over.
176: The XL is something of a legend in Discraft’s history — one of the earliest “long but controllable” drivers that bridged the gap between distance and finesse. It earned fame when Scott Stokely set a 693 ft distance record using one, solidifying its place in disc lore. Today it’s often seen as a straight-to-slight fade driver with surprising torque tolerance; in many hands it behaves more like a neutral fairway with added stretch. It doesn’t demand raw speed to use, and for many players it becomes the “go straight and see what happens” option on risk-reward holes.
177: The Cyclone is a bit of a classic throwback — it lives in that space between midrange and fairway driver, delivering a hyzer-flip to flat profile with moderate fade. In its era it was one of the trailblazers for smaller diameter drivers, and you’ll see echoes of its handling in many modern molds. For many throwers it’s less “go hard, go far” and more “line it up and let it fly,” especially on controlled shots. It tends to get more forgiving with use, gaining a bit more turn while retaining a smooth fade toward the end — making it a cherished mold for those who value finesse over brute force.
178: The Latitude 64 Striker is a control fairway driver built for accuracy and consistency, with enough stability to handle power while still offering a smooth, workable flight. It holds a straight line with a dependable fade, making it ideal for tight fairways, tunnel shots, and controlled placement drives. The Striker has a comfortable rim and a glidey profile, but it resists turn far more than understable options in the lineup. Compared to the Saint Pro, it offers a slightly straighter mid-flight with similar wind-fighting reliability. Though it’s no longer in regular production, the Striker has maintained a loyal following thanks to its clean release, shaping ability, and trustworthy finish.
179: Discraft’s Stalker (PDGA-approved June 17, 2009) is the quintessential straight-control fairway many players call a “longer Buzzz.” Its narrow, comfortable rim and subtle micro-bead keep lines honest and ground play tame, making it a tunnel-shot and low-ceiling specialist with soft, “hit-and-sit” landings. Give it a touch of hyzer and it pops to flat, tracks forever, then fades gently; power it down for placements or up for laser-straight hyzer-flips without fear of sudden bite. The mold’s had spotlight runs—think early Paige Pierce signatures and Hailey King Tour Series—but the Stalker’s enduring charm is simple: trustworthy, point-and-shoot control when you absolutely must thread the fairway.
181: The Latitude 64 Saint is a speed 9 driver known for its glide and finesse, making it a favorite among players who value control just as much as distance. It offers a gentle turn with a dependable fade, perfect for shaping long fairway lines or threading wooded gaps. Easy to hyzer-flip and capable of holding an anhyzer, the Saint excels for intermediate throwers and advanced players alike. While not built to fight heavy wind, its workability and glide make it a go-to for calm-day drives. If you’re chasing effortless distance with precision, the Saint answers the call.
187: The Latitude 64 Jade is a glide-rich control driver designed as a step up from the Diamond, offering a bit more stability without sacrificing ease of throw. It launches into a clean hyzer-flip, holds straight well—even in light wind—and finishes with a gentle fade. Its generous glide helps extend throws, particularly uphill or through wooded fairways, allowing players with moderate arm speed to maximize distance and control. Many users appreciate how it handles more power than the Diamond while maintaining a reliable fade, and some note it quietly outperforms expectations in both glide and consistency. Comfortable in the hand, it’s equally friendly to backhand and forehand shots. The Jade shines as a dependable shaping tool—ideal for S-curves, hyzer-flips, or finesse drives—making it a go-to for athletes progressing beyond beginner molds who still value accuracy.
188: The Latitude 64 Fury is a glide-packed, understable control driver designed as the next step up from the Diamond for players craving more distance without giving up ease. It launches with a smooth hyzer-flip, cruises straight even in moderate wind, then finishes with a gentle fade—perfect for long S-curves, turnover lines, or controlled rollers. Many users find it more controllable than similarly understable discs like the Sidewinder, thanks to stronger glide and lane-holding stability. Plastics like GL and Opto are praised for providing durability without sacrificing that signature turn-to-fade path. It’s a reliable utility driver that adapts across skill levels—great for beginners stepping up, and still a trusted shaping tool for experienced flex and turnover shots.
210: Latitude 64’s XXX is an old-school meat hook—one of the brand’s earliest truly overstable fairways—built for spike hyzers, skip shots, and headwinds that would make gentler discs cry. Typically flat and very torque-resistant, it became a forehand favorite for players who want a short, sharp finish with minimal glide and predictable ground play. In the woods it works as a point-and-dump placement tool; in the open it’s your “turn the corner now” disc. The XXX eventually faded from regular production as newer molds like the Pioneer took over the slot, but loyalists still swear by its utility, durability, and that satisfyingly abrupt fade. If control is king, the XXX rules by decree.
211: Latitude 64’s Spark was designed with—and originally fronted by—David Feldberg as a workhorse overstable fairway you could trust in wind, on forehands, and for point-and-dump placements. PDGA-approved in April 2015, it earned a following for its typically flat top, torque resistance, and utility lines like thumbers and steep spike hyzers, while run chatter often noted Opto as the beefier starter and Recycled beating straighter a touch quicker. In Latitude’s lineup it effectively bridged the gap between stable control drivers and true meathooks, before newer molds took over that slot. The Spark was officially retired in early 2025, but loyal throwers still swear it sparks confidence when precision matters.
213: From Latitude 64: Ballista Pro is the big brother to the Ballista, with added stability for experienced players. It is the perfect solution if you are looking for a distance driver that can navigate tight fairways. With a great combination of speed, stability, and glide it is the go-to disc for all kinds of distance shots.
215: A steady, dependable fairway driver, the Explorer is engineered for controlled, precise lines rather than wild distance pushes. It offers a straight flight path with just enough finish to hold a reliable fade, making it a go-to when you want accuracy over aggression. Many players treat it as a “workhorse” — it’s a disc you can trust when you need consistency in tricky fairways and it also handles subtle hyzer-flips when it’s slightly beaten in. Over time it loses a bit of its edge, becoming easier to flip-up without losing that dependable finish.
217: Latitude 64’s Diamond is the gateway gem of their Easy-to-Use lineup, PDGA-approved in 2011 and intentionally molded mostly in lighter weights (roughly mid-140s to high-150s) so newer or slower-speed throwers can get effortless glide, easy hyzer-flips, and gentle turnovers without wrestling a wide rim. It became a staple recommendation for kids, seniors, and anyone learning clean form, while power arms keep one for touchy woods lines or cheeky rollers. Over the years Latitude has even released occasional “170+ Carat” runs for players who love the Diamond flight but want a bit more wind resistance. Think of it as the sparkly sibling to Ruby and Pearl—friendly, workable, and still one of the safest first drivers you can hand someone.
256: From Westside Discs: The World is our fastest high speed driver. Designed as a distance driver the World gets there fast and flies great close to the ground. It has a low profile and a great feel. For professional players it is the fastest disc on the market that holds a hyzer line for anyone. For lower speed arms the World will be the disc in your bag that is over stable and fast in all conditions. You can count on the World to get you further down the fairway right away.
259: The Prodigy H3 V2 is a retooled hybrid driver that blends speed, glide, and control. Compared to the original H3, the V2 sports a slightly flatter top and refined rim for better hand feel and a more consistent release. It offers a reliable straight flight with subtle turn and a dependable fade, making it a go-to for controlled distance drives and shaping lines. Great for both backhand and forehand throwers who want accuracy without sacrificing distance.
260: From Westside Discs: Like its namesake, this is made to cover long distances. This is a super-high speed disc that even the big arms will be able to use. Fast with enough stability to really handle a full power throw. When you need to go a long way with predictability, launch this Catapult over any obstacle in your way.
261: The Prodigy H1 V2 is a retooled overstable hybrid driver introduced in 2018. This design offers increased glide and distance while maintaining the dependable overstability that power throwers and forehand specialists rely on. Its a go-to choice for headwinds, flex lines, and skip finishes, delivering consistent performance in demanding conditions.
263: Our most popular high speed driver, the Westside King is our fastest disc for all levels of players. The farthest flying disc in our line the King is designed to allow the average player to experience a long distance flight. It has a good grip and a nice high dome. It traps the air and rides on it like you have never seen before. For professional players the King will be your longest flying disc and roller in your bag. For lower speed arms this will finally give you that full flight you always wanted on the course.
264: The Prodigy H5 is a hybrid control driver that’s refreshingly easy to flick and fun to master. It reliably flips up from a hyzer and glides straight as an arrow—or threads just enough turnover to chase through tunnels or pick up a roller. Perfect for players growing into bigger arms, yet skilled enough for rollers and finesse hyzer-flips. One Redditor says it's “pretty dang understable… a nice roller/woods disc,” while another noted it goes “hyzerflip to flex” with surprising distance . Its predictable flight makes it a go-to for open fairways or tight wooded lines. And hey, if your bag only carries one hybrid? The H5 might just end up having a fan club.
266: A strong Queen has the same qualities as that of a King, just in a smaller package. This Queen is just as fast as its counterpart but has a noticeably smaller feel in the hand. Great as a bomber or a stand still surgical instrument. The Queen will rule your bag with the right mix of grace and power.
268: Two things are undeniable about this disc - speed and glide. This beauty really gets out there. For the higher arm speeds, a powered down throw will still get out to great distances. For the lower arm speeds, this will be your long range bomber. Everyone can find a way to throw the Destiny. You will just have to walk a long way to go pick it up.
279: The Boatman is a fast, slightly overstable distance driver with a comfortable rim and dependable fade. It offers a long glide and a consistent finish, making it suitable for players seeking a reliable driver that can handle various conditions. Compared to the Innova Wraith, the Boatman provides a straighter flight with a touch more stability, offering a balanced option between control and distance.
284: The Sword is a high-speed distance driver designed for players seeking long, controllable flights. It offers a balanced combination of glide and stability, making it suitable for shaping various shot lines. Players have noted that the Sword can hold lines well and provides a predictable finish, making it a reliable choice for both backhand and forehand throws.
285: The Westside Discs Fortress is a speed 10 control driver introduced in 2017, designed to offer a balance of speed, control, and stability. It excels in headwind conditions, providing a reliable flight path with a consistent fade, making it suitable for both backhand and forehand throws. The Fortresss design allows for long fairway drives, hyzers, and flex shots, offering versatility for various shot shapes. Its comfortable grip and dependable performance make it a valuable addition to many players bags.
286: The Westside Discs Northman is a versatile distance driver that offers a balanced flight, making it suitable for a wide range of players. With its moderate speed and neutral stability, the Northman provides consistent, accurate drives. For players with faster arm speeds, it delivers a straight flight with a gentle fade at the end. Those with slower arm speeds will find it to be a dependable, stable disc that maintains its line well. The Northmans comfortable rim and reliable performance make it a valuable addition to any disc golfers bag.
288: The Westside Discs Ahti is a flat-topped, overstable fairway driver made for power throws, sharp fades, and fearless flights in any wind. Its dependable finish and torque-resistant design make it a favorite for forehand specialists, big hyzer lines, and low, skipping approaches. The Ahti doesn’t glide much—it just punches forward and dives hard, exactly when and where you expect it to. Players often reach for it when placement is more important than distance, especially on tight or windy courses. If you’re looking for a disc that sticks the landing and never turns over, the Ahti gets the job done.
289: The Westside Discs Longbowman debuted in 2022 as a high-power, overstable distance driver designed for commanding control in all conditions. It offers a flat profile and grippy rim that empower players to launch sharp hyzer bombs, low forehands, and headwind shots with confidence. Compared to Westside’s Kaxe, the Longbowman steps up in torque resistance and fade, making it a go-to when you need precision placement and minimal drift. It’s not built for glide-happy flights—this is a disc that punches forward and sticks the landing. For players seeking a wind-defying utility bomber, the Longbowman is a steadfast ally.
290: The Westside Discs Sampo is a speed 10 fairway driver introduced in 2015, designed for players seeking a neutral flight with dependable control. With its moderate glide and slight turn, it excels in long, straight shots and low-ceiling lines, making it suitable for both backhand and forehand throws. The Sampo's design allows it to hold hyzer lines effectively and resist turning over in headwinds, providing a reliable option for various shot shapes. Named after a mythical artifact from the Finnish epic Kalevala, the Sampo connects disc golf with Finland's rich storytelling heritage. Special editions, such as the Tournament Orbit Sampo, have been released to celebrate this cultural connection.
291: The Westside Stag is a glidey, moderately overstable fairway driver that excels at shaping controlled lines with a touch of finesse. It offers just enough turn to carry straight before finishing with a smooth, reliable fade. The Stag is especially popular in wooded fairways, where its combination of glide and control lets it thread tight gaps without fading out too early. Compared to the Bear, the Stag is less overstable and more forgiving at lower power, making it easier to shape hyzer-flips and gentle S-curves. It also shares some characteristics with the Saint Pro but feels a bit less sharp on the finish. For players looking for a fairway driver that rewards clean form and touch without sacrificing reliability, the Stag delivers a balanced, confident flight.
292: This is the listing for the old DD2, produced when Discmania was manufactured by Innova. This version of the DD2 never really took off. The DD2 has since been reinvented to replace the Enigma (another discontinued disc). The new DD2 is actually supposed to be almost exactly an Enigma.
296: The Westside Hatchet is a versatile, easy-throwing fairway driver that excels at straight shots, gentle turnovers, and approachable rollers. It offers smooth hyzer-flips that hold flat and finish with a dependable fade, making it ideal for technical fairways where control matters more than speed. Many players appreciate its understable flight and surprising glide—easy to work right out of the box without needing to beat it in. Whether carving S-curves through the woods or laying down placement drives, the Hatchet rewards clean form and angle control. A reliable, no-fuss option for players seeking finesse and shapeability over raw distance.
297: The CD3 is Discmania’s 11-speed control driver, offering a balanced blend of speed, glide, and control. With flight numbers of 11/5/-1/2, it provides a touch of high-speed turn followed by a reliable fade, making it suitable for shaping various lines. While the CD3 is currently out of production, players seeking a similar flight experience might consider the DD1, which shares comparable flight characteristics.
298: The PDx is Discmania’s overstable distance driver that bridges the gap between the PD and PD2. It offers the speed and fade of the PD2 with the control of the PD, making it ideal for headwinds, flex lines, and power forehands. Released initially as a fundraiser disc, the PDx later became available in C-Line plastic. Though now discontinued, it remains a favorite among players seeking reliable overstability without the extreme demands of higher-speed discs.
300: The original Discmania CD (Control Driver) was designed to bridge the gap between fairway and distance drivers, offering dependable control with sneaky distance. Released in the early 2010s, the CD was beloved for its neutral-to-slightly-understable flight, making it a go-to for hyzer flips, long turnovers, and straight shots that finish with a touch of fade. It never reached the popularity of molds like the FD or PD but gained a cult following among players who prized its glide and workability. Though replaced by later iterations like the CD2 and CD1, the original CD still holds a soft spot for Discmania loyalists and collectors alike.
303: From Legacy Discs: The Cannon’s older brother, the Rampage is a high speed over stable driver. This mold is designed to withstand the wind, holding its flight pattern even into a headwind. Designed for those with greater arm speed, the Rampage is faster than anything you’ve previously thrown. Extremely quick off the tee, with a slight turn as it glides, the Rampage finishes strong at the end of its flight. Definitely for the power thrower.
307: The Outlaw is essentially the Legacy Discs version of the Destroyer. High speed, slight turn, solid overstability - a good formula for a consistant distance driver.
310: Discmania first released the FD3 in July 2015 as their most overstable fairway driver—immediately filling a gap for players needing wind-proof, torque-resistant control. Its low-profile, concave rim allows for powerful backhand throws and smooth sidearms, with a straight flight that reliably finishes hard. Compared to Discmania’s Power Driver (PD), it offers noticeably stronger stability, and players appreciate it for both hyzer shots and headwind bombs. The FD3’s overstable nature makes it a go-to utility disc, ideal for tight wooded lines or gusty fairways. If it’s windy or you need a dependable fade, the FD3 delivers every time.
312: The Legacy Nemesis lives up to its name—if your nemesis is straight fairways that refuse to yield. Designed for big-turning drives and effortless distance, the Nemesis thrives on hyzer-flips, long turnovers, and rollers that just won’t settle. It’s a finesse driver at heart, perfect for players with developing arms who still want that full-flight flex. For power throwers, it becomes a shot-shaping tool that dances around obstacles and sneaks through tight lines. Think of it as a Mongoose with a little more attitude and speed—easy to trust when you need to turn heads and turn corners.
313: The Discmania TDX is a sleek, glidey understable control driver that feels like a faster CD‑line fairway with a slightly wider rim. It’s easy to throw flat or on hyzer into dependable turnovers, long S-curves, and rollers, making it an ideal go-to for players who don’t generate max arm speed. Its forgiving flight is especially popular among those seeking utility in both open and wooded fairways. Though technically a 9-speed, many find it more neutral in practice, offering predictable carry and soft fade. Over the years it's earned a cult following, with users praising its comfortable grip and consistency compared to similar fairway molds. If you want a dependable turnover tool that’s fun to shape, the TDX delivers without surprises.
326: The Legacy Bandit is a straight‑flying, understable control driver that outpaces intermediate fairway molds without demanding elite power. It responds well to both slight hyzer and flat releases, offering smooth S‑curve lines or gentle turnovers depending on your arm speed. Many describe it as more flippy than expected—best used on hyzer flips to tame its understability rather than blasting flat into headwinds. It delivers reliable glide and a mild finish, making it a solid choice for shaping shots and long fairway drives. Ideal for players seeking a user‑friendly 9‑speed with finesse and finesse.
328: The Rival is often spoken of as a Teebird analogue — a reliable straight-to-fade fairway driver that bridges control and distance. It tends to have less glide than some of its peers, which helps it stay on line rather than ballooning in headwinds. In the hands of experienced throwers, it’s often chosen for midrange distance shots where precision matters more than outright speed. Some players mention the Rival feels stiff or somewhat firm — its durability is solid, but high stiffness can give a harsher release in cold or slick plastics.
330: The Legacy Phenom is a stable fairway driver designed for control and accuracy. It offers a comfortable, slightly rounded rim and a smooth release, making it a solid choice for shaping lines in tight fairways. The flight leans straight with a gentle fade at the end, holding angles well without being overly sensitive to power. It's especially useful for players who want a dependable fairway option that bridges the gap between glide and control.
333: The Legacy Enemy is a powerhouse overstable fairway driver built to laugh in the face of wind. Think of it as a Firebird with extra biceps—great for sharp hyzer shots, forehand blasts, and reliable sky placement. It flies fast, resists glide, and finishes hard, making it a go-to when you need your disc to land right where you aim. One fan said it “flies like a FAF Champ Firebird… but it feels better in the hand,” while another swears by it as “the wind’s worst enemy.” If your bag needs a dependable, no-nonsense wind warrior, the Enemy’s got your six.
339: The Legacy Mongoose is a control-focused fairway driver designed for precision over raw speed. It delivers straight, stable flights with a smooth, dependable fade—ideal for tunnel shots, technical lines, and placement drives. Under higher arm speeds it offers just a touch of turnover before settling in, making it a versatile option for players still refining power but eager to shape a variety of shots. Many users appreciate its comfortable feel and consistency; it won’t surprise you by flipping over or dumping hard. A popular comparison is to mid-range shells—except the Mongoose goes farther while retaining mid-level forgiveness. It’s a reliable go-to for players seeking a straight, trusty fairway driver that blends finesse with added distance.
347: The Prodiscus Legenda is a high-speed, overstable distance driver with dependable fade, ideal for strong throwers and windy conditions.
353: Disc golfers can charge into battle with the new overstable distance driver from Westside Discs, the War Horse. Combining higher speed with dependable stability, the War Horse can tackle strong winds with pinpoint precision.
356: The Prodiscus Laseri is a control driver known for its straight, no-nonsense flight and pinpoint accuracy. It’s faster and more neutral than the RESPECTi, with less fade but still enough stability to trust on flat releases. Great for tight fairways, low ceilings, and laser-straight drives where you don’t want the disc to drift or dive.
359: The Prodiscus Flipperi is a very understable control driver that lives up to its name—ideal for hyzer-flips, long turnovers, and reliable rollers. 361: Fast and overstable even in extreme wind situations. You can trust Thunder God Thor to fade! 376: The Daredevil Wolverine is a dependable stable-to-overstable fairway driver released in early 2007. Need a predictable fairway workhorse with glide and grip? The Wolverine won’t disappoint.
379: The Timberwolf is a reliable control/fairway driver that stays remarkably straight before settling into a soft, predictable finish. Whether you’re an intermediate or advanced thrower, the Timberwolf earns its stripes as a line-locking workhorse you can count on.

383: The Daredevil Discs Sabertooth is a seriously overstable fairway driver designed to tear through headwinds and deliver powerful, dependable fades. 386: The Daredevil Discs Buffalo is a grippy, overstable distance driver designed for wind resistance with a touch of turn early on.
