Whether you're dialing in precision or just need a fairway driver that holds the line, the TL3 delivers.
1499: The Thought Space Athletics Coalesce landed in early 2022 as TSA’s Goldilocks fairway driver—just the right balance of straight flight and dependable fade. Unlike their ultra-overstable Omen, it offers enough stability to resist headwinds while still allowing finesse hyzer-flips and flex lines. Players and reviewers praise its flat top and comfortable beadless rim, noting its performance spans 250‑ to 500‑foot shots with consistent results, backhand or forehand. One fan described it as a “longer, straighter fairway driver with serious finishing power.” If you want a reliable, versatile workhorse that thrives in varied conditions, the Coalesce is a standout pick.
1500: The Axiom Wrath launched in 2015 as a stable-to-overstable driver in the 18.5 mm rim family, offering a straighter alternative to the beefier Fireball or Motion. It bridges the gap between stable fairways and torque-resistant distance molds—ideal for players who want reliability without sacrificing carry. Mid-speed throws will fly smooth flex lines before a firm fade, while high-speed efforts translate to locked-in finishes even in wind. Compared to the Tesla, the Wrath is noticeably more grounded, but it remains approachable and consistent. If you’re after a dependable utility driver for controlled distance and powerful placement, the Wrath earns its name.
1508: The Sage is a fast, glidey distance driver that blends power and control. It has just enough turn to shape long flights and finishes with dependable fade. Great for players looking to stretch their distance without jumping to something too overstable. Crafted in Clash’s grippy, durable Steady plastic for consistent feel and performance.
1512: The Idog from Kastaplast is an intriguing mold that leans toward the manageable side of control drivers. It works well when you want to finesse your way through gaps rather than brute your way. Its design gives it a fair balance: it resists flipping at high speed yet softens enough to open gentle hyzer-flips in the right hands. Among Kastaplast’s lineup of often very stable molds, the Idog positions itself as the “patient, controlled forward flyer” — a quieter tool for precise shaping.
1515: The Streamline Shift is a highly understable 9-speed fairway driver that excels at hyzer-flips, long turnovers, and easy rollers. It’s surprisingly glidey and forgiving—even modest power arms can toss it straight with a late, controlled finish. As it beats in, the Shift becomes floppy enough to reliably turn over on flat tees, yet still holds enough structure to smooth out S-curves when aimed on anhyzer. Many users reach for it as a trusty utility tool rather than a go-to bomber—ideal for shaping wide sweeping lines or low rollers. It shines in woods or open fields where finesse matters more than distance, offering predictable flight without the unpredictability of more stable molds. In short, the Shift is a friendly, versatile shape driver that fits a wide range of play styles.
1521: The Gateway Aura is a high-speed distance driver designed for players seeking long, controlled flights with a touch of understability. Crafted as the less-stable sibling to Gateway's Realm and Spell, the Aura excels in hyzer flips and turnover shots, providing a reliable option for shaping various lines on the course. Its flight characteristics make it suitable for players of all arm speeds, offering a balance between distance and control. The Aura is available in multiple plastic blends, including Platinum and NXT, catering to different preferences for grip and durability. Overall, the Gateway Aura stands out as a versatile distance driver that combines speed, glide, and a workable turn, making it a valuable addition to many disc golf bags.
1522: The Lone Star Cactus is an understable distance driver built for effortless hyzer flips and controlled turnovers. It's a natural fit for players stepping up from fairways who want added glide without punishing fade. Often compared to discs like the Innova Sidewinder or Discraft Heat, the Cactus holds smooth S-lines with minimal effort. While it’s a newer release in Lone Star’s growing lineup, it’s quickly earning a spot as a go-to for shaping lines through wooded fairways or maximizing distance on tailwind shots.
1524: The Lone Star Desperado is a smooth, glidey fairway driver that blends ease and finesse. With a touch of understability, it gently turns on a hyzer flip and finishes with a clean, reliable fade—ideal for long, controlled S-curves or rollers. It handles slower arm speeds well, flying neutral until it kicks out, but with more power you can shape gentle turnovers with confidence. Many players compare its feel and flight to a Leopard3 but with noticeably better glide and straighter carry. It's user-friendly for beginners seeking distance and enjoyable for seasoned throwers who want a dependable shaping tool in the woods or open fairways. The Desperado rewards accuracy over power and stands out as a versatile control driver that many find they reach for again and again.
1526: The Birdie Disc Supply Weapon is an overstable fairway driver designed for power and precision. It launches solidly on hyzer or flat, resists any high-speed turn, and delivers a consistent, firm fade—ideal for battling wind, tight fairways, or shot shapes that demand authority. Its slightly wider rim provides a confident grip and reliable torque resistance, making it a favorite for forehands and controlled backhand placement shots. While it’s not built for maximum distance, it excels in utility roles: placement shots, strong wind hyzers, and lines that rely on control rather than glide. A dependable option when you need a driving weapon you can trust every time.
1536: The Expanse is Thought Space’s first-ever collaboration with Discraft, pairing bold TSA design with Discraft’s trusted molds. It’s a glidey, slightly understable distance driver built for shaping smooth, soaring lines—perfect for players who like their throws to look as good as they fly.
1537: The Gateway Odyssey is a unique control—or fairway—driver that brings innovative over‑molded construction into play. Its dual‑material design balances weight between the rim and flight plate for impressive straight‑flying performance and precision. It’s known for a friendly, understable flight with smooth turnover and a soft finish, making it a great pick for shaping lines, hyzer‑flips, and gentle S‑curves. It’s a disc that rewards clean release and control more than raw power.
1540: Gateway’s Hybrid is a slightly overstable fairway from the mid-2000s (PDGA-approved October 2, 2005) that was brought back into the spotlight with a 2022 Premier Box drop. True to its name, it bridges the Sabre and Blaze: more bite and wind-friendliness than a Sabre, without the dumpy finish of a Blaze. The rim feels compact and confident for both backhand and forehand, excelling on low-ceiling lasers, corner-turning hyzers, and “point-and-park” placements. Recent runs in Hyper Diamond tout a slimmer profile and “Surface Technology” that adds a touch of extra stability and release consistency, while SureGrip versions tend to start a hair straighter. If you like fairways that mind their manners—and finish on command—the Hybrid earns its spot.
1541: The Gateway Amphibian is a smooth-flying control driver with a surprising trick: it floats on water—even at max weight—thanks to its thicker flight plate and etched rim. That extra buoyancy makes it great for creek-side play or rainy rounds. With a gentle turn and soft fade, it effortlessly holds long hyzer-flip lines, drifts through tunnels, or tucks into a partner-style roller. Beginners appreciate its friendly flight path, while experienced players lean on it for tech shots or dependable rollers. It’s a disc that hops into your bag—no frogs required—and sticks around because it does exactly what it promises.
1543: The Typhoon is a stable distance driver co-designed by 2X World Champion Catrina Allen, positioned between the Rogue and the Hurricane in DGA's lineup. It offers exceptional glide and moderate fade, making it suitable for controlled hyzer-flips and forward-skipping maximum distance shots. With its comfortable wide rim and beadless design, the Typhoon provides a smooth, consistent flight, allowing players to shape long turnover shots and execute precise flex lines with confidence. The Typhoon is available in various plastic blends, including ProLine and Experimental Blend, catering to different preferences for grip and durability.
1545: The Skyway is a stable distance driver designed by 12-time World Champion Ken Climo. With flight numbers of 11/5/-1/3, it offers a balance of distance and control, making it suitable for players of all skill levels. The Skyway delivers impressive glide and a reliable finish, excelling in both forehand and backhand throws. Its design is inspired by the Sunshine Skyway Bridge, reflecting elegance and strength in its flight characteristics.
1552: The Cigarra is a deliberate “overstable evolution” of Discraft’s Cicada, co-designed with Anthony Barela. Its name literally means “cicada” in Spanish — a choice that nods to both its lineage and Barela’s heritage. Unlike the original Cicada (which leans toward turnover and soft finishes), the Cigarra is tuned to hold up under power: it flips into longer, straighter lines and finishes with more authority. It bridges the gap between Cicada’s finesse and the bold control required by stronger throwers. In contour, it feels familiar — but its behavior pushes harder, especially on hyzer-flips and stand-up forehands.
1553: The Kastaplast Malm is a 10-speed overstable fairway driver designed to bridge the gap between the Stål and Guld in Kastaplast’s lineup . It offers a reliable fade and torque resistance, making it suitable for both backhand and forehand throws, especially in headwind conditions. The Malm's flight characteristics provide a dependable option for players seeking control and stability in their distance shots. Released on April 3, 2025, the Malm is available in both K1 and K1 Hard plastics, with the first run featuring a special Tour Team stamp . Its name, meaning "ore" in Swedish, reflects Kastaplast's tradition of metal-themed disc names and pays homage to the malmar districts of Stockholm.
1557: The Dimension balances overstable resistance to turn while allowing a full flight before fade. Strong throwers will see only the smallest turnover at high speeds or into headwinds. Average throwers will get all the overstability they desire from this speed class in the Dimension. With its ultra-fast speed and glide-promoting dome, the Dimension’s reliable fade helps pinpoint your target from a great distance.
1558: The Tantrum’s sweeping lines and hyzerflip potential allow power throwers to shape all kinds of shots. The Tantrum is best described as a beat-in Teleport, with huge glide and distance potential.
1559: From Innova: The Firestorm is a wide-rimmed, speed 14 distance driver that some would describe as a faster, beat-in Destroyer. On low, level drives thrown with enough speed, the Firestorm flies straight with a forward-finishing fade.
1561: The Energy is designed to resist power and headwinds, it will handle the hardest throws into the hardest winds and yield predictable golf flights. As the overstable bookend to the 23mm class, the Energy shares its core and shallow dome with the Nitro. When you’re going for max distance above all, the added dome and glide are useful — with the superb line-holding properties of GYRO™, the Energy can take advantage of this glide without sacrificing its wind resistance.
1562: Nitro falls in the general stability lineage of Servo, Volt, Tesla, and Photon, with a turn-resistant profile that covers ground and guarantees a fade finish. Average throwers may need lighter weights or headwinds to achieve what little turn is offered by Nitro, while power throwers will find a workable and responsive shallow turn.
1563: The Panic is thoroughly overstable, with plenty of beef to handle headwinds and torqued-up sidearms. Its overstability holds the Panic on any kind of hyzer line and allows steep anhyzer flex shots. For high-power throwers, the Panic will be a useful utility driver, while newer and average throwers will get an extremely overstable flight. The Panic is best described as a seasoned MVP Nitro.
1564: The Teleport’s straight-stable design produces a tight S-curve at high speeds, with plenty of stability to keep it headed toward its target. While high-power throwers and headwinds can produce these shallow turnover lines, average throwers will get a long and manageably resistant driver in the Teleport. Within the context of the 24.5mm class, Teleport has the most distance potential for the most throwers in the core distance slot.
1565: The Excite is able to achieve long accurate distance with ease from its high amount of glide and ability to hyzer-flip straight with a lower power requirement. Power throwers will be able to send this max-speed driver on huge turnover lines with a late-ending fade or attack the course with high-speed rollers. The Excite’s flight characteristics emulate the Insanity but with added speed and even more glide potential.
1566: The younger brother of the Rampage, the Cannon is another high speed driver. This disc will come off the tee every bit as fast as the Rampage, though with a strong turn and lengthy glide. The Cannon also has a much slower fade at the end of its flight, providing for the longest flight in the market. The Cannon will be replacing most high speed drivers out there.
1567: The Axiom Defy is a stable-overstable distance driver known for its resistance to turnover and reliable fade. Positioned as a more stable counterpart to the MVP Photon, it offers a straighter initial flight with a stronger finish, making it suitable for both forehand and backhand throws. Its consistent performance in various conditions has made it a dependable choice for players seeking a trustworthy driver.
1568: The Photon is MVP’s stable-to-overstable distance driver, offering a reliable fade and wind resistance. It’s often described as a longer Tesla, providing consistent performance for power throwers. Ideal for both forehand and backhand throws, the Photon excels in headwinds and delivers dependable distance.
1572: Thought Space Athletics’ Persona is an understable fairway built for easy hyzer-flips and late-drifting turnovers in the woods, officially PDGA-approved on March 3, 2025. It’s also one of the first TSA molds manufactured by Discraft following their early-2025 partnership, launching in TSA’s Vex blend with a comfortable, moderate rim that suits touch shots. Early player chatter pegs it as notably flippy—even for modest arms—so clean release and nose control are rewarded; power throwers can milk effortless stand-ups, gentle anhyzers, and cheeky rollers. For TSA fans, it naturally slots under the Mantra in stability, offering a true finesse option when you want glide and shape over bite (and a little personality to match its name).
1585: From Westside: Ride the waves of precision and power with the Westside Tide, a high-speed driver crafted for those who seek effortless distance and unwavering control. With exceptional glide and balanced stability, Tide is the perfect companion for players who demand both reach and accuracy. Whether attacking long fairways or shaping masterful shots, this disc is ready to elevate your game.
1593: While the Atom in baseline plastics is just the slightest bit understable, the flight numbers are actualy different for premium plastics like Proton. The Proton Atom has the flight numbers 3/3/0/1.
1594: The #1 putter. The Aviar Putt & Approach is the beadless version of the Aviar, which is the most common. There are versions of the Aviar that are beaded, like the Yeti Pro, JK Pro, and KC Pro Aviars.
1595: The Classic Aviar is beadless just like the Aviar P&A. With a turn and fade of 0, the Classic Aviar is the most neutral version. As opposed to the regular Aviar P&A which has a slight fade of 1.
1597: The Banger GT is a GREAT throwing putter. It has a nice flight just for putting too. The thing to remember is that GT stands for Grip Track, meaning that the Banger has a big thumb slot that runs around the flight plate. I think it feels super comfortable in the hand, but its certainly a matter of preference.
1600: The Beetle is one of the OG hybrid catch discs. It's shapped more like a frisbee than a disc, it's just small in diameter like a disc. Great for floaty drifting shots and approaches, but the insanely high glide also makes it not the best choice for putting.
1601: The Berg was the 1st of its kind. The flight plate is extremely puddle-topped on every single Berg, a special part of the design that brings the glide levels way down. The Berg is the ultimate approach disc. It holds any angle of flight without turning or being squirrelly, and it never wants to fly very far.
1602: The Berg X is a modified Berg that's just ever so slightly more overstable than the Berg. Anyone who wants that slight increase from the Berg is destined for the Berg X.
1612: The first putter to arrive in Ken Climo's lineup, manufactured by Discraft. The mold shape is eerily similar to a beaded Aviar.
1624: One of the most popular discs to come out in the last few years. Everyone needs a Glitch. Whether or not it's a good disc to use during a round is still up for debate. But even if you don't enjoy throwing buttery approaches, having this disc in your bag for a game of warm-up pass can come in clutch.
1634: The Hydrogen arguably started the influx in 1-speed disc popularity. Before releasing, Løft Discs claimed that it would be the straightest flying putter in all of disc golf. It could very well be that - if thrown with good form, it glides dead straight, and is neutral enough to hold lines on either hyzer or anhyzer. Because of it's lid-like feel and shape, the Hydrogen never really caught on with mainstream disc golfers. But without the initial hype and popularity, would we ever have seen the Glitch, Pitch, Parachute, or Spore?
1654: The Nova is one of the straightest, truest, best throwing putters that money can buy. Whether you're just starting out, or a seasoned master, the Nova can revitalize your game by teaching you how to throw smooth. If the Nova isn't flying great and straight, than you know you need some work.
1660: The P1-Ace! Simon Lizotte used to love throwing his P1X. The P1X was also the putter of choice of Paul Krans before his switch to MVP. It\'s beaded, and very very very straight.
1661: The P2 could possibly have been the most popular putter at one point in time. The P2 was used by many touring pros, such as Paul McBeth, Eagle McMahon, Simon Lizotte, Nate Sexton, and more. Originally molded off of the Aviar, the P2 was always sligtly more overstable. Nowadays, there\'s a TON of putters that are just trying to emulate the P2!
1662: The P2X came into the lineup after the addition of Gannon Buhr to Discmania's Sky Team. Gannon putted with Links for a while before the release of the P2X. The P2X has a similar overstability to the P2, but it has a bead. It almost exactly resembles Prodigy's famous PA3 putter, which is funny cause that's what Gannon used to putt with.
1668: The most popular disc of 2024 and 2025! The Pixel was released as a part of the Simon Line, a special line of Axiom made just for Simon Lizotte with his input heavily weighed into the design. The Pixel is super glidey, super straight, and a spin putters absolute dream disc.
1676: The one and only... People go nuts over the Polecat. When Innova first started making Halo Star plastic, they were spammed with requests to make Halo Star Polecats. Innova gave in, and did a spcial run of Halo Star Polecats that burned the popularity even further. They now do tournaments where you can only throw a Polecat the whole round! As far as cults go, this is a good one.
1681: Eagle McMahon's special putter from his days with Discmania. Essentially a beveled down P2, the Rainmaker ended up being an incredible straight flying putter. I may even argue that it should actually be listed as a speed of 3, just because of how far and fast this disc glides. Availability has been spotty at best since Eagle's departure. No word has come in about whether or not it will be rereleased.
1699: If you've watched Garrett Gurthie throw in a little 80 foot anhyzer through the woods, than you've seen the Sonic in action. It's one of the easiest to throw Putt & Approach discs out there (although we wouldn't recommend that you use it for putting, it's a throwing putter or approach disc for sure).
1714: Possibly the greatest beaded putter in all of disc golf. The Wizard is the most popular disc to come from Gateway, and has been for the past 20 or so years. Its consistant but slight overstability give it a predictable drop towards the end of its flight.
1716: When Innova made discs for Discmania, there was a disc called the P1X. Simon Lizotte used to throw one a lot, he referred to it as his P1-Ace. It's not officially official that the P1X is the same mold as the Xero, but not long after the Discmania split Innova suddently released the Xero and it's basically identical to the P1X. Xero, P1X, whatever, it's a great putter.
1728: The DD2 has returned to Discmania’s Originals line, retooled from the Enigma mold previously part of the Evolution series. This updated DD2 offers high-speed distance with a touch of turn and a dependable fade, making it a versatile option for players seeking long, controlled flights. The first release of the retooled DD2 is available in Horizon S-Line plastic, known for its premium feel and durability. This special edition was introduced as part of the 2025 PDGA World Championships fundraising efforts.
1731: The Lark was one of Stokely Discs’ earlier fairway driver entries, tailored toward accessibility. Its design is meant to fly straight with a slight, predictable fade — ideal for intermediate throwers or players stepping into fairway drivers. Because of its forgiving profile, it’s often one of the first molds people try when upgrading from midranges. Users describe it as reliable: not overly aggressive, not undercut, but dependable for lines where you can’t afford surprises.
1732: The CHING Strato Precision, now revived by Stokely Discs, is a glidey, straight-flying midrange that excels at controlled finesse shots. Whether youre threading wooded gaps or dialing in approach lines, this disc delivers buttery-smooth precision with a touch of old-school charm.
1734: The Doomsday Discs Blackout is an understable fairway driver designed for controlled, glidey flights with minimal fade. With a speed rating of 8, it offers a comfortable rim and clean release, making it ideal for precise placement shots and navigating tight fairways. The Blackout excels at holding the line you put it on, whether you're executing gentle hyzer-flips or smooth turnovers. Its versatility and reliability make it a go-to disc for players seeking consistent performance across various shot types.
1735: The Doomsday Discs Desolation is an overstable midrange designed for consistent, torque-resistant performance. It offers a straight flight with a dependable fade, making it ideal for controlled approaches and navigating tight fairways. The Desolation features a comfortable, beadless rim and is available in various premium plastics, including Biohazard and Toxic Waste, each offering distinct grip and flexibility characteristics. As part of Doomsday's Catastrophic Line, the Desolation is a reliable choice for players seeking a versatile midrange that performs well across different conditions.
1736: The Doomsday Discs Crisis is an overstable approach disc designed for precision and reliability in challenging conditions. With a flat top and beadless rim, it offers a comfortable grip and a consistent, dependable fade, making it ideal for controlled approaches and navigating tight fairways. The Crisis excels at holding the line you put it on, whether you're executing gentle hyzer-flips or smooth turnovers. Its versatility and reliability make it a go-to disc for players seeking consistent performance across various shot types.
1737: The Doomsday Discs Solar Death Ray is a unique fairway driver that combines distinctive design with versatile performance. Featuring concentric flight rings on the top of the flight plate, it offers enhanced grip and a tactile feel reminiscent of vintage discs. With a neutral flight path, the Solar Death Ray provides an understable turn followed by a smooth fade, making it ideal for hyzer-flips, tunnel shots, and controlled drives. Its comfortable rim and reliable performance make it suitable for players of all skill levels.
1738: The Doomsday Discs Area 51 is an overstable approach disc designed for precision and torque resistance. Its shallow, beadless profile offers a comfortable grip, making it ideal for both backhand and forehand throws. With a flight similar to the Discraft Zone but featuring a shallower feel, the Area 51 excels in controlled approaches and headwind putts. Available in various plastics, including the base-level Ration and the premium Clandestine, it caters to different grip preferences and durability needs. As part of Doomsday's Conspiracy Line, the Area 51 combines reliable performance with a unique thematic flair.
1740: The Doomsday Discs Bleak is a beadless putter known for its straight, glidey flight and clean release. With a shallow rim and comfortable hand feel, it excels in both circle putting and controlled approach shots. The Bleak offers a neutral flight with a touch of turn and minimal fade, making it versatile for various throwing styles. Available in multiple plastic blends, including the grippy Ration and durable Survival, it caters to different preferences and conditions. Whether you're navigating tight fairways or aiming for the chains, the Bleak provides consistent performance and reliability.
1741: The Doomsday Discs Famine is an understable distance driver designed for players seeking maximum distance with minimal effort. With its high-speed turn and gentle fade, the Famine excels at long hyzer-flips, turnover shots, and rollers. Its flight characteristics make it ideal for players with slower arm speeds looking to achieve greater distance, as well as advanced players aiming for controlled shot shaping.
1742: The ABC Discs Flying Squirrel is an understable midrange disc renowned for its exceptional glide and user-friendly flight characteristics. Designed with a beadless rim and a distinctive concave underside, it offers a comfortable grip for backhand throws, though some players may find the rim shape less suited for forehand grips. Ideal for beginners and intermediate players, the Flying Squirrel excels at hyzer-flips, turnovers, and navigating tight fairways with precision. Its ability to hold anhyzer lines and execute smooth curves makes it a versatile tool for shaping shots and achieving controlled distance on the course.
1747: The Kastaplast Tuff is a small-bead putter with a rounded, finger-friendly profile and noticeably more glide than Kastaplast’s Reko. It’s stable to slightly overstable, offering excellent torque resistance—making it reliable for both straight putting and forehand approaches. Its clean release and consistent flight path give confidence from the circle to mid-range upshots. A solid choice when you want predictable, glidey control in any putting or approach situation.
1752: Enter the Dino Discs Pterodactyl —a whimsical, lightweight distance driver that’s the perfect first flight for young or low-power players. Its slim, easy-to-grip rim means you don’t need Hulk-level arm strength, and it floats in water, so losing it to a creek won’t sting as much. Designed as a gateway disc, it flips up cleanly and glides straight, offering a taste of distance without demanding precision. Some players note that in even mild wind it’s a bit too feathery—think “whisper-light”—but on calm days it’s a blast. Bonus: it looks and feels like a real driver, just featherweight fun!
1760: Streamline’s Turbulence is an overstable fairway introduced in 2025 and PDGA-approved on May 19, 2025. Its calling card is a purposefully concave flight plate—borrowed from Streamline’s Range mid—that deliberately lowers glide and boosts torque resistance, producing a cleaner forehand/backhand release and tighter distance control. On course, that means headwind confidence, spike-hyzer accuracy, and muted ground play when you need it to sit. Thrown flat it tracks forward before a quick, reliable finish; powered down it becomes a point-and-dump placement tool for corners and tight woods gaps. Launch runs arrived in Neutron with a dense, secure feel. When you want precision over carry, kick up some Turbulence..
1763: Approved on April 28th, 2025, the Above Ground Level Elm is AGL’s first Innova-made disc—and a big shift in their lineup. It's a flat, overstable fairway driver built for forehand torque, headwind control, and precise hyzer placement. But here’s the twist: it’s widely believed to be a rebranded FD3 mold, giving players that familiar, beefy fairway feel with a new leaf-wrapped identity. Compared to AGL’s softer and more understable lineup, the Elm is a total outlier—in the best way. If you’ve wanted AGL flight with Firebird-style finish, the Elm delivers that with Innova consistency behind the scenes.
1765: Dynamic Discs Motive is a breezy, understable fairway disc that’s like a “tunnel-shot cheat code” for players unlocking gentle turnovers and hyzer-flips, all while still offering a dependable late fade that keeps it from drifting away. It’s got a comfy, approachable rim—not too wide—which makes it especially friendly for lighter arms or headwinds, and early runs even include those coveted sub-150 g options so it floats straight and controlled. Forehand lovers dig how it cruises out smooth, and back-hand throwers appreciate how it shapes thoughtful gentle S-curves in wooded lines with ease—perfect for dialing in those graceful placement shots with minimal effort and maximum flow.
1790: Named after the Brazos River in Texas, this fairway driver embodies Lone Star’s regional identity — straight-flying, confident, and versatile. Released during the company’s rapid expansion of molds, the Brazos filled a crucial gap between their slower control discs and more aggressive drivers. Its flight offers the kind of steady glide and neutral stability that fits nearly any skill level, especially on wooded or technical courses. As Lone Star gained traction nationally, the Brazos became one of its most reliable “Texas straight” offerings — practical, confident, and true to its roots..
